A critical function of AV fleet management is the strategic positioning (or pre- positioning) of empty AV fleet vehicles in anticipation of surge flows—whether from unusual demand (such as a special event) or in response to a modal interface (such as transfers from a regional train or banks of arrivals at an airport). Other critical AV fleet management functions are associated with traditional traffic management centers that direct resources in response to unusual traffic conditions and incidents on roadways. For AV fleets, this includes not only any vehicle-associated crash or individual vehicle ADS system failure but also an additional layer of rider/occupant interaction (a function typically performed by the driver in manned operations) and remote operation/intervention whenever the vehicle experiences a condition outside the bounds of its operational design domain. AV fleet management and its automation to minimize personnel resources while optimizing user experience and consistency of experience—referred to herein as ASDC—is increasingly being acknowledged as a critical next frontier for realizing the benefits of AMDs. As an AMD scales the operation of multiple fleets of automated passenger transport systems (both public and private) within the defined boundaries of the district, each with its own AV technologies—as illustrated in Figure 22—adds to the complexity of management and operations. In addition to automated passenger service, the district may also include automated cargo/package delivery fleets as well as legacy manual vehicle fleets for public transit. This yields the previously referenced system-of-systems characteristic for the AMD and its supporting infrastructure. Each fleet will have unique vehicle technology, with the size and configuration of each fleet selected to optimally serve its market sector. The latter is expected to be the dominant mode, especially for short trips within an AMD. With respect to on- demand service mode, Phase III research reviewed several analytical simulation studies of conceptual ATN systems that operate primarily in a demand-response fashion. These ATN simulation studies dating to the 2000s revealed that on a typical network with many stations, most of the trip demand involved trips between only a subset of the overall stations. It was found that these high-demand station pairs were often better served by larger vehicles, whereas smaller vehicles were suited for the many other station pairs with low trip demands. Further, these high- demand station pairs may also be effectively serviced with fixed-route operation during all or part of the day, though not necessarily on a fixed schedule. Fully automated supervisory and dispatch control systems are well suited for adapting the vehicle assignments of varying vehicle sizes and modes (fixed route and on demand) as the demand changes throughout the day.
